title: Fringed garter scarf
subtitle: A plain garter scarf finished with knotted fringe on both short ends.
excerpt: A straight garter-stitch scarf on 5 mm needles with aran yarn, finished with a knotted fringe of yarn lengths threaded through the cast-on and cast-off edges. Finished dimensions are 18 cm wide by 170 cm long plus approximately 12 cm fringe.
sourceNotes: Fringed scarves and shawls are documented throughout Weldon's Practical Knitter; the knotted fringe technique is described in Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870) for shawls and wraps. Cornelia Mee, A Manual of Knitting and Crochet (1846), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: Decorative yarn lengths attached to the edges of a knitted piece by folding a bundle of strands in half, inserting the loop through an edge stitch, and pulling the cut ends through the loop to form a knot.
A cast-on using the tail and working yarn together to form an elastic, neat edge.

content.text: This is a straight garter-stitch scarf worked flat on 5 mm needles with aran yarn, finishing at 18 cm wide and 170 cm long with a knotted
fringe
of approximately 12 cm attached to both short ends. The fringe is added after casting off and takes about 30 minutes.

Flat construction is straightforward for a garter scarf. The fringe is attached by threading folded yarn strands through the edge stitches and knotting them, which is faster and more secure on garter stitch than on stocking stitch because the edge loops in garter are consistently sized. The finished scarf uses about 190 g (340 m / 372 yards) of aran-weight yarn, including fringe.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.qty: 190 g total (approx. 340 m / 372 yards, including fringe)
items.substitutions: Reserve about 25 g for fringe, or use a contrast yarn colour for the fringe.

items.name: Small crochet hook (4 or 5 mm)
items.substitutions: Fingers work; a hook makes attaching fringe tidier.

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 36 rows = 10 x 10 cm in garter stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. Each stitch off gauge changes the finished width by about 1 cm; each two rows off gauge across the full 612-row scarf adds or removes about 5 cm of finished length.
Stitches used
K (knit). Every row is a knit row.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on
to place 32 stitches. Tail length: (15.7 x 32) / 10 + 15 = about 65 cm.
Stitch count check-in: 32 stitches after the cast-on.
Body
Every row: K to end. (32 sts)
Continue until the scarf measures 170 cm from the cast-on edge, measured flat. This takes approximately 612 rows. At the halfway mark (85 cm), count: still 32 stitches.
Cast off
Cast off using the standard method. Work loosely.
Fringe

Cut yarn lengths of 28 cm each (they will fold to 14 cm and knot to approximately 12 cm of hanging fringe). For each fringe bundle, take two or three lengths together, fold in half, insert the crochet hook (or your fingers) from back to front through an edge stitch, draw the folded loop through, then pull the cut ends through the loop and tighten the knot.
Attach fringe bundles every four stitches across both short edges (approximately eight bundles per edge). Trim to an even length after knotting.
Common faults
Fringe bundles pulling loose after washing. Ensure the loop is tightened firmly before trimming. On a garter edge, pulling the knot against the outermost ridge locks it well.
Fringe uneven after trimming. Cut fringe lengths over a ruler or a piece of card to get consistent 28 cm lengths before attaching. Trim the finished fringe against a ruler held flat.
Tight cast-off that makes the fringe bunching along the top edge. Work the cast-off row with a needle one size larger.
Finishing
Weave in any yarn tails not used for fringe. Wet block the body of the scarf before attaching the fringe: the fringe does not need blocking.
Care

Handwash wool in cool water. Gently squeeze the fringe and lay the scarf flat to dry. Avoid wringing, which tangles the fringe. After drying, comb the fringe lightly with fingers to separate any bunched strands.
What to try next
The colour-block scarf extends the garter technique to a two-colour piece. Or try the striped scarf for a slightly more involved colour change at each end.
